# Object-Relational Model

A relational database with user-defined types layered on top: rows are objects, columns can be
pointers to other objects, types carry methods, and a join becomes a dot. Oracle's implementation is
the reference one; the ideas are older than any of the ORMs that reinvented them in application code.

## The three moves

1. **`CREATE TYPE … AS OBJECT`** — a structured type with attributes and `MEMBER FUNCTION` /
   `MEMBER PROCEDURE` declarations, plus a separate `TYPE BODY`.
2. **`CREATE TABLE … OF type`** — a typed (object) table. Each row *is* an instance, addressable by a
   `REF`.
3. **`REF type`** — a pointer column. `DEREF(r)` returns the whole object; `alias.col.attr` navigates
   in one step; `VALUE(t)` returns the row object itself.

In [[oracle-database-laboratories]] the entire cat-herd domain is rebuilt this way as `cat_type`,
`common_type`, `elite_type`, `account_type` and `incident_type`, alongside — not replacing — the
relational schema. The two coexist in one schema, which forces the naming discipline: `CatsR`,
`IncidentsR`, and `_r`-suffixed constraint names, because Oracle constraint names are unique per
schema rather than per table.

## A join becomes a dot

```sql
-- relational
SELECT c.name FROM Cats c JOIN Cats chief ON c.chief = chief.nickname;

-- object-relational
SELECT c.chief.name FROM CatsR c;
```

The second is shorter, and that is the whole sales pitch. It is also strictly less flexible: the
navigation direction is fixed by which side holds the pointer, and there is no `LEFT JOIN` equivalent
— a `NULL` `REF` simply yields `NULL`. Traversal still works: `CONNECT BY` runs over `REF`s once
resolved to a comparable attribute, so [[hierarchical-queries]] carries over unchanged.

## `SCOPE FOR` is the load-bearing detail

> "SCOPE FOR constrains the REF to one table. Without it a REF may point at any table of the type,
> the pointer needs more storage, and Oracle cannot resolve dot navigation as efficiently."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/04_object_relational/01_types_and_tables.sql, 2026-07-25

Three benefits from one clause — smaller pointer, faster navigation, and a correctness guarantee that
the pointer cannot stray to an unexpected table of the same type. An unscoped `REF` is a foreign key
with no target table named, which is not a thing the relational model would ever have allowed.

## What the model does *not* give you

- **Dangling references are possible.** Delete the row a `REF` points at and the pointer survives its
  target. `IS DANGLING` is the only reliable test. A foreign key would have refused the delete or
  cascaded it; a `REF` does neither by default. This is the single clearest reason the relational
  model is still the default.
- **Methods run per row.** `get_total_eats()` puts the `NVL` arithmetic on the type instead of at
  every call site — genuinely better than repeating it — but it is a function call per row, not a
  set operation.
- **Type signatures must match their bodies exactly.** Declaring `RETURN DATE` over a `TO_CHAR` body
  makes Oracle convert the string back through the session's NLS format: silent on a matching
  session, `PLS-00382` on any other. The file names this trap where it occurs.
- **`SELF` is `IN OUT` by default** in a `MEMBER PROCEDURE`, so assigning to an attribute mutates the
  instance the caller holds. Convenient and easy to miss.

## The honest assessment

The object-relational layer buys terser navigation and lets domain logic live with the data. It costs
referential guarantees, portability, and a second set of teardown rules — object tables must be
dropped before the types they are built on, since `FORCE` would leave the table invalid rather than
removing the dependency. Compare {{database-normalisation}}: the relational model is a set of
guarantees you give up piece by piece, and each concession should be named.
